title: Can Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Configurations? A Paired, Validator‑Grounded Study
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces executable unsafe network configurations produced from natural‑language intents. After an autonomous literature review and preregistered paired design, we ran a confirmatory experiment (N=200 paired intents) using a single initial LLM generation per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics) from gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network configuration validator with a single permitted repair iteration. All 200 initial candidates were reused for both baseline and guarded conditions; the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied. Result: baseline valid = 200/200 (100%), guarded valid = 200/200 (100%); paired difference = 0.0 (exact McNemar p = 1.0). Interpretation: on this synthetic, validator‑scored task set the GVR pipeline produced no measurable improvement because the shared initial candidates were already validator‑valid; the experiment therefore demonstrates successful end‑to‑end execution and deterministic scoring but does not provide evidence that GVR reduces misconfiguration rates in broader or real operational settings. We report full preregistration, execution artifacts, and an explicit discussion of threats to validity (task realism, shared_initial_candidate semantics, single model, temperature unset).

sections.introduction: Motivation: Large language models (LLMs) are being proposed for intent‑driven NetOps tasks such as translating natural‑language intents to device configurations. Hallucination and unsafe outputs are well documented in LLM literature and operational AIOps work; verifier‑guided pipelines that generate, validate, and repair candidate artifacts have been proposed to improve correctness in IaC and related domains. Research question: Does a GVR pipeline combining an LLM generator and a deterministic NetOps validator reduce the rate of executable unsafe or incorrect network configurations relative to the raw initial LLM generation? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment design under shared_initial_candidate semantics; (2) an autonomous, reproducible execution on N=200 paired intents using gpt-5-mini with deterministic validator scoring; (3) transparent reporting of execution artifacts and a calibrated interpretation that acknowledges the design constraints that produced a null effect.
sections.related_work: LLM unreliability and hallucination are core concerns for operational applications and motivate evidence‑grounded generation (surveyed across domains) [1]. Retrieval‑augmented and evidence‑grounded pipelines reduce hallucination in some AIOps-style QA and doc tasks [2]. Generate–validate–repair architectures have been shown to improve correctness for Infrastructure‑as‑Code generation when coupled with verifiers and iterative correction [3]. Prior NetOps studies demonstrate LLM capability benchmarks and intent‑translation prototypes, but execution‑level safety evaluations (model→verifier→simulator) are underrepresented in the literature and motivate this focused empirical study [4]. (Cited records used to position this study are enumerated in the disclosure.)
sections.methodology: Preregistration: We froze the study (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) before any model calls. Design: paired binary confirmatory test comparing baseline (single initial candidate accepted as-is) versus guarded (same initial candidate validated and permitted one automated repair) per intent. Generation semantics: shared_initial_candidate — exactly one LLM sample per intent was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. Model and provider: declared model gpt-5-mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (model_configuration.json). Temperature was null/unset in the archived configuration; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling. Task bank: 200 deterministic synthetic NetOps intents (intent_configuration_repair_v1 family) selected prior to execution; selection and contamination checks were preregistered. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied to candidate configurations to produce binary valid/invalid labels and to record repair attempts. Execution: adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed 200 shared initial generations (model_calls_used=200) and produced 400 scored episodes (baseline+guarded), with full artifact capture (provider traces, validator traces, simulator final states). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Primary test: exact two‑sided McNemar on paired 2×2 table; sensitivity and exploratory analyses specified in the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution and raw artifacts: execution manifest and analysis artifacts archived (execution completed 2026‑09‑01). Model calls used: 200 (one shared initial generation per intent). Scoring outcomes (deterministic validator): baseline valid = 200/200 (100%); guarded valid = 200/200 (100%). Paired contingency table: n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Confirmatory test: paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0] under the preregistered bootstrap. No repairs were applied in any guarded episode because validator reports were valid before repair. All preregistered exclusion, contamination, and missingness checks passed (no excluded or missing pairs).
sections.discussion: The experiment executed the preregistered pipeline end‑to‑end and demonstrates that deterministic validator scoring and artifact capture can be integrated with hosted LLM generations under strict reproducibility controls. The null result (no measurable GVR benefit) follows directly from the preregistered design and the shared_initial_candidate semantics: the single sampled candidate reused across conditions was already validator‑valid for all tasks, so downstream repair had no opportunity to change outcomes. This outcome is scientifically informative at two levels: (i) it validates the experimental infrastructure, artifact capture, and deterministic scoring; (ii) it highlights that shared_initial_candidate designs can produce paired null differences when initial candidates are valid, and therefore such a design cannot measure improvements arising from generating alternate first‑pass candidates. Threats to validity: internal — shared_initial_candidate semantics (paired comparison only tests post‑generation validation/repair), temperature unset in model configuration (not evidence of deterministic sampling), single model (gpt-5-mini) and single validator; construct — synthetic task bank and validator abstractions may not capture all real device behaviors or complex vendor CLI semantics; external — single model, synthetic tasks, no live hardware execution; conclusion validity — absolute sample size sufficient for the preplanned effect but uninformative when observed baseline success=100%. Implications: evidence supports that a reproducible GVR evaluation pipeline is feasible, but additional experiments are required to probe settings where initial LLM candidates produce nontrivial validator failures (e.g., sampling multiple candidates, higher‑temperature sampling, different models, or more adversarial/realistic intent sets).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a GVR pipeline reduces executable unsafe LLM‑generated network configurations. In this run (N=200 pairs, shared_initial_candidate), all initial candidates were valid under the deterministic validator and no repairs were applied; thus the guarded pipeline showed no improvement relative to baseline (paired difference 0.0). The study establishes an end‑to‑end, artifacted evaluation workflow and documents important experimental semantics (shared_initial_candidate, temperature unset) that shape interpretability. Future work should (a) evaluate multi‑sample generation semantics (independent per‑condition sampling), (b) test higher‑temperature/heterogeneous models, (c) broaden task realism and validator fidelity (vendor CLIs, runtime simulation/emulation), and (d) analyze failure categories and repair efficacy where the validator actually flags candidate faults.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory): This study was executed under an autonomy boundary defined by a human Research Director who selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) prior to the autonomy lock. After the lock the autonomous system performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting without human manual editing of technical content. Models and tooling: the declared model was gpt-5-mini (provider adapter 'openai_responses'); hosted adapter calls produced the shared initial generation samples. The archived model configuration shows temperature=null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0. Generation semantics: the preregistered and executed design used shared_initial_candidate semantics — exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions; no independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling was performed. Preregistration reference: PREREG-CAND-001-VER-GVR-2026-09-01 (preregistration manifest archived and referenced in the execution manifest). Execution artifacts: the experiment ran under adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and completed with model_calls_used=200 and completed_episode_count=400 (200 paired tasks). Validator and repairs: a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) scored candidates and a single automated repair iteration was permitted; in this run the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied. Autonomy and human role: pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred (as permitted by the Master Prompt); those pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence in this final run. After the autonomy lock no human manually rewrote technical results, manuscript text, figures, or references. Master prompt reference (immutable archived path and SHA‑256): provenance/master_prompt.txt — 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Deviations: none of the preregistered confirmatory controls that would have altered the analysis were changed post‑hoc; all execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single sampled initial generation was reused across baseline and guarded conditions; this design measures validator/repair downstream effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition generation strategies.

Temperature unset (temperature=null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt-5-mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic intent_configuration_repair_v1 items with deterministic validator scoring; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed in live devices or exhaustive vendor emulators.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects task/ sampling conditions rather than proof that GVR is unnecessary in general.

External validity: absence of live hardware/emulation execution and limited task diversity constrain operational generalizability; follow‑on studies should expand model diversity, sampling regimes, and validator fidelity.
